title: How A* finds the shortest path

lines: You click on the map, and your character walks there, around every wall. How does it find the way?
Many games do it with a method called A-star. Let us watch it work.
First, cut the map into squares. Green is the start. Gold is the goal. Grey squares are walls.
The simple way is to search like water. Check every square one step away, then two steps away, and so on.
Keep going until the water reaches the goal.
This gives the shortest path. But look how many squares we had to check, even far from the goal.
A-star is smarter. It gives every square a score, made of two numbers.
The first is g: the steps we walked from the start to reach this square.
The second is h: a guess of the steps still left. Just count the squares to the goal, as if there were no walls.
Add them, and you get f. f equals g plus h. It is our guess for the whole trip through this square.
A square that leads away from the goal gets a high f. A square on the way gets a low one.
Now one rule. Look at the squares on the edge of the search. Always open the one with the lowest f.
At first, the search runs straight at the goal, because those squares have the lowest f.
Then it hits the wall. Every step to the side makes f grow. So the search spreads, layer by layer, until it finds a way around.
At the goal, it follows its steps back to the start. That is the path, and your character can walk it.
Now put the two side by side. Same map, same start, same goal.
Both find a shortest path. But here A-star checks far fewer squares, because h pulls it toward the goal.
One warning. The guess must never be too high, or the path may not be the shortest. Ours ignores the walls, so it is never too high.
To sum up. g is the steps already walked.
h is a guess of the steps left.
A-star always opens the square with the lowest f, g plus h.
So next time a character walks around a wall, you know how it found the way.
